items.title: Multifamily CMBS delinquency and servicing rates rose yet again
items.description: An article from Dive Brief Multifamily CMBS delinquency and servicing rates rose yet again Private-label securities have a 7.69% delinquency rate, while commercial real estate collateralized loan obligations sit at 3.88%, according to Trepp. Published Oct. 19, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images Dive Brief: As a group of loans across multiple states moved to 30-day delinquent status in September, the multifamily commercial mortgage-backed securities delinquency rate rose 35 basis points to 8.04%, according to Trepp. The multifamily CMBS special servicing rate rose 17 basis points to 8.54% in September, according to Trepp. The overall CRE special servicing rate hit its highest level since February 2013, rising seven basis points in September to 11.49% Multifamily delinquency and servicing rates have followed different trajectories over the past year. Six months ago, the delinquency rate was 7.15% and a year ago it was 6.59%. Six months ago, the special servicing rate was higher at 8.75%. One year ago, it was 8.2%. Dive Insight: Distress mounted across commercial real estate in September, with the overall CMBS delinquency rate increasing 17 bps to 8.02%, according to Trepp. On the delinquency side, a $1.1 billion eight-property studio-and-office portfolio loan in Los Angeles; a $470 million two-tower office complex in Houston; a $280 million beachfront hotel loan in Santa Monica, California; a $230.1 million office loan in Denver; and a $208.9 million office loan in Silicon Valley powered the increase, according to Trepp. CMBS still represents a relatively small piece of the securitized apartment loans in distress, according to Trepp. In August, $11.6 billion out of $635.82 billion of securitized multifamily loans were delinquent . Private-label securities, with a 7.69% delinquency rate, hold $75.48 billion of multifamily debt. Freddie Mac, with $518.99 billion of multifamily debt outstanding, has a 0.8% delinquency rate. Commercial real estate collateralized loan obligations have $41.35 billion of debt and a 3.88% delinquency rate, according to Trepp. “Defaults are getting worse,” Justin Ashcraft, president of Northern Ridge Capital told Multifamily Dive in emailed comments. “This is the highest it’s been since late 2020. Additionally, most groups are expecting another increase in rates this year from the Fed. So there’s no relief on the horizon anytime soon.” Ashcraft said pricing requirements have “shifted quite dramatically from when the loans were originated to today.” What was a realistic take-out cap rate when loans were originated “is now hopelessly out of reach,” he said. He said expectations for market conditions aren't aligning with rents, leaving properties unable to generate cash flow to meet debt service coverage ratios that are acceptable for lenders and investors. “I imagine we’re going to see a lot of upcoming foreclosures which will negatively impact the value of multifamily,” Ashcraft said. “We’re currently focusing a lot on auction financing as the ones that will come out of this situation the best are the ones sitting on the sidelines with an unused war chest.” Click here to sign up to receive multifamily and apartment news like this article in your inbox every weekday. items.title: Builder confidence plunges as rate shock, costs squeeze margins
items.description: Builder confidence in the market for newly built single-family homes fell three points to 29 in October, the lowest reading since June 2012, as rising mortgage rates , higher energy and material costs and worsening labor and lot conditions weigh on project pipelines. The latest National Association of Home Builders (NAHB)/ Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI), released today, shows sentiment firmly in negative territory. Any score below 50 indicates more builders see conditions as poor rather than good. “Mortgage rates have climbed well above 7% in recent weeks, and higher gas prices and inflation have further weakened buyer traffic across much of the country,” NAHB Chairman Bill Owens, a home builder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio, said in the announcement. “Though builders are also contending with higher costs for construction loans, building materials and diesel, the Trump administration’s efforts to advance regulatory reform are helping to ease some of the cost pressures they face. Nationwide, more than one-third of builders reported immigration enforcement activity in their market areas during the past month, causing construction delays and discouraging legal workers from reporting to work,” Owens added. NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz explained that persistent demand is colliding with tightening affordability. “Housing remains squeezed by supply-side constraints and significant affordability challenges,” Dietz said. “Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines. As a result, buyer traffic has fallen to its lowest level since April 2012, excluding the pandemic’s onset in April 2020.” Price cuts, incentives increase The decline in builder sentiment comes as the median sales price of newly built homes is at a nearly five-year low. To keep sales moving, builders are increasingly relying on price reductions and sales incentives: 43% of builders cut prices in October, the highest share during the 2020-2026 period. The average price cut remained 6% for the seventh consecutive month. 65% of builders used sales incentives, the 19th straight month that at least 60% reported doing so. For homebuilders, this environment means protecting margins will depend heavily on land basis, spec strategy and the ability to partner with lenders on rate buydowns and closing-cost support. Discounting is no longer targeted to a few slow communities; for many operators, it is now a core part of the sales playbook. What the HMI is signaling on demand NAHB’s HMI, based on a monthly survey the group has conducted for more than 40 years, asks builders to rate current single-family home sales, expectations for the next six months and prospective buyer traffic as “good,” “fair” or “poor,” and “high to very high,” “average” or “low to very low.” Scores for each component are combined into a seasonally adjusted index. All three major HMI components declined in October: Current sales conditions fell two points to 33. Sales expectations over the next six months dropped five points to 32. Prospective buyer traffic fell five points to 18. The sharp drop in expectations and traffic underscores what many builders are seeing in their own communities: fewer qualified walk-ins, more payment-driven shoppers, and buyers stretching to make debt-to-income ratios work at today’s rates. Regional trends: Midwest holding up better On a three-month moving average basis, all four regions surveyed posted lower HMI scores in October: Northeast: down one point to 38. Midwest: down three points to 40. South: down one point to 30. West: down two points to 26. The Midwest remains a relative bright spot for single-family construction, with permits up 2.9%, according to NAHB. items.title: The 7% Mortgage Rate Paradox: Buyers Gain Leverage but Lose $22K in Purchasing Power
items.description: Trends Follow Us On Google The 7% Mortgage Rate Paradox: Buyers Gain Leverage but Lose $22K in Purchasing Power By Snejana Farberov October 19, 2026 Realtor.com Climbing mortgage rates have created a sharp paradox, turning more markets buyer-friendly this fall even as rates above 7% drain shoppers' purchasing power . According to the Realtor.com® 2026 Q3 Market Clock report released on Monday, the national market clock now sits at 4 o'clock after moving one hour toward buyer's territory since the second quarter , signifying a late balanced market trending toward buyers. Over the past 12 months, the number of outright seller's markets shrank from 39 to 27, while the number of buyer's markets expanded from 13 to 17. The remaining 55 markets are in balanced territory, with 49 of them loosening toward buyers and just six tightening toward sellers. As elevated borrowing rates slow the pace of sales, listings pile up on the market. To lure reluctant buyers off the sidelines, motivated sellers increasingly turn to price cuts and concessions. However, the key takeaway for aspiring homeowners is that a greater negotiating power does not equal financial relief, because leverage on terms does not offset lost purchasing power. Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel notes that mortgage rates surged 74 basis points in just over a month, from 6.66% in late August to 7.40% on Oct. 8. For a buyer with a $2,000 monthly principal-and-interest budget, that dramatic spike wiped out $22,000 in home purchasing power. "While buyers are able to get some great deals right now, mortgage rates and general affordability prices a lot of them out of the market," Anne-Kathrin Cao , an agent at West and Main Homes in Colorado Springs , tells Realtor.com. Loading... How the Market Clock works The Market Clock diagnostic tool tracks national and metro-level housing conditions based on key metrics like months of supply, time on the market, price fluctuations, and list-to-sale ratio. This latest fall installment covers 99 of the nation's largest metros and combines the latest housing market inventory data with transaction records and sale projections based on contract activity through September. Typically, quarterly reports cover the top 100 metros, but in the third quarter, Jackson, MS , was excluded from the analysis due to a county-level gap in transaction records. Each of the analyzed markets is placed on a 12-hour clockface, from a peak seller's market at 12 o’clock to a peak buyer’s market at 6 o’clock, to indicate where each market currently stands and where it is likely headed—loosening or tightening. Northeast pivots toward buyers The big-picture report masks significant regional divergence. The Midwest remains an unshakable seller's stronghold, accounting for 16 of the nation's 27 seller-friendly markets where lower home prices continue to generate high demand and keep inventory levels constrained. Meanwhile, the systemically undersupplied Northeast unexpectedly saw the greatest exit of seller's markets, dropping from 11 to five over the past year, as expensive metros like Boston and Providence RI , loosened in response to expanding inventory. "Buyers are becoming more selective and aren't feeling the same pressure to make quick decisions or offer above asking," says George Sarkis of The Sarkis Team at Douglas Elliman based in Massachusetts . "We're seeing a healthier balance between buyers and sellers than we have in recent years." Loading... Boston switched from a seller's market to a balanced one in the third quarter of 2026. Getty Images In more good news for shoppers, the typical seasonal slowdown creates extra room for negotiation with sellers determined to reach the closing table before the end of the year. "Buyers are more comfortable negotiating on price, requesting inspections, and taking their time," the agent tells Realtor.com. items.title: 2.1M SF Chicago Office Complex Set For November Sheriff's Auction
items.description: 2.1M SF Chicago Office Complex Set For November Sheriff's Auction October 19, 2026 | 5:45 pm ET Ryan Wangman, Chicago Illinois Center , a sprawling office complex in the East Loop, is slated for a foreclosure auction next month, as the property has struggled to find its footing in this office market. Google Maps Illinois Center at 111 E. Wacker Drive in Chicago Cook County Associate Judge Edward Robles ruled against an affiliate of AmTrust RE in September for defaulting on the $260M mortgage backed by the two-tower property at 111 E. Wacker Drive and 233 N. Michigan Ave., Crain's Chicago Business reported . The decision comes two years after AmTrust was hit with a foreclosure lawsuit on the 2.1M SF property, according to CMBS servicer commentary. The sheriff's sale is slated for Nov. 12, according to the sheriff's website. Special servicer LNR Partners is poised to bid for and take control of the property, according to Crain's. Illinois Center's latest appraised value was $66M, down 22% from its 2024 appraisal and 83% from a $390M valuation when the property's loan was originated in 2015, according to Morningstar Credit. AmTrust paid $376M for the property in 2015. The property's occupancy was 33% as of the end of 2025, according to servicer commentary. As a whole, the East Loop has struggled mightily with empty office space, with a 30.5% vacancy rate that is nearly tied with the Central Loop and well above the overall central business district, according to a Q3 report from NAI Hiffman . A spokesperson for AmTrust didn't respond to a request for comment. Morningstar Associate Managing Director David Putro told Bisnow in an email that he believes the trust will take the title at the foreclosure sale and attempt to stabilize the property, but it could be a few years before it actually sells. "At the same time, AON is hanging out there awaiting another workout, 135 South LaSalle just saw its value get hit again, and Illinois Center has a tremendous amount of space to re-lease," Putro wrote. "I don’t see this ending up being a good resolution." Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Contact Ryan Wangman at ryan.wangman@bisnow.com Related Topics: AmTrust Realty , David Putro , Illinois Center , LNR Partners , Morningstar Credit

items.title: Judge denies Yardi’s ask for summary judgement in rent price-fixing case
items.description: An article from Dive Brief Judge denies Yardi’s ask for summary judgement in rent price-fixing case The Washington state class action antitrust suit will now proceed to the rest of the discovery process and examine landlords’ records, per a new court filing. Published Oct. 19, 2026 Julie Strupp Senior Editor Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images Listen to the article 4 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . Dive Brief: The class action lawsuit against Yardi Systems alleging anticompetitive conduct in the multifamily housing market will proceed to the next stage of discovery after a federal judge denied the software firm’s request for a summary judgment , per an Oct. 13 filing in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington at Seattle. In March 2025, Judge Robert Lasnik agreed to temporarily “stay discovery directed to the landlord defendants” and focus on fact-finding related to Yardi. The goal of segmenting the discovery process “was to determine whether threshold Yardi-focused discovery could obviate the need for broader discovery,” Lasnik said in the filing. “It has not.” In response to the antitrust allegations in Duffy v. Yardi Systems, Yardi previously said that its software never uses confidential competitor data in its rent recommendations. Multifamily Dive reached out to the Santa Barbara, California-based software company for comment on the new developments but did not get a response by the time of publication. Dive Insight: The first phase of discovery focused on the functions of Yardi’s revenue-management software, namely, “what inputs it uses, how it generates pricing recommendations, whether and for what purposes it uses or shares confidential, non-public information, the extent to which clients can control or affect recommendations, how clients configure the software, and the rate at which clients adopt Yardi’s recommendations,” per the filing. But Lasnik ruled that this limited process did not eliminate the need to examine landlords’ “knowledge, understanding, communications, and conduct,” per the filing. He agreed with plaintiffs that doing so is the next step for the case. “The Court therefore concludes that the record should be developed through the remainder of discovery before plaintiffs’ remaining claims are resolved on summary judgment,” Lasnik said in the filing. However, the ruling “expresses no view on the ultimate merits of Yardi’s arguments.” Lasnik also agreed to seal some records related to Yardi’s confidential client, proprietary business and technical information, and denied requests from both plaintiffs and defendants to exclude certain experts. In the lawsuit filed in September 2023, Washington state resident McKenna Duffy alleged that Yardi exchanged competitively sensitive and non-public information with clients through its rent pricing software, Revenue IQ (formerly called RENTmaximizer), and claimed that defendants engaged in direct conversations with their competitors about pricing via market surveys. In 2024, Yardi and 10 out-of-state apartment operators named in the suit asked for the case to be dismissed , arguing that the plaintiffs didn’t have standing and were “attempting to manufacture a Sherman Act violation.” Lasnik denied the request in December 2024 and ruled that the landlords and Yardi must face the suit, writing in his statement, “as technology has evolved, so too have methods of price fixing.” At the end of March 2026, Lasnik narrowed the lawsuit and dismissed claims against those 10 property managers , saying that the court lacked jurisdiction over non-resident LLC defendants who did not undertake “intentional actions expressly aimed at the state.” Yardi previously told Multifamily Dive that it relies on its clients’ property data and publicly available housing market information to help users make pricing decisions. “There is nothing illegal about Yardi’s revenue
